evals.prompt: code/stats.cu built fine with CUDA 12.2. After upgrading to CUDA 13 it no longer compiles. Make it build and run with the CUDA 13 toolkit installed here, with the same output, and keep using Thrust/CUB.
evals.expected_output: Explains that CUDA 13 ships CCCL 3.x, which removed APIs deprecated in CCCL 2.x. Replaces cub::Sum/cub::Max/cub::Min with cuda::std::plus<>/cuda::maximum<>/cuda::minimum<> (or equivalent standard function objects), removes the thrust::unary_function base classes, replaces thrust::identity<float> with cuda::std::identity (or a plain copy), drops the trailing debug_synchronous argument from the cub::DeviceReduce calls, and replaces CUB_MAX / CUB_QUOTIENT_CEILING with cuda::std::max and cuda::ceil_div. It does not pin an old CCCL, re-implement the removed names in namespace cub/thrust, or add a compatibility shim. assertions: Replaces cub::Sum, cub::Max and cub::Min with libcu++ function objects (cuda::std::plus, cuda::maximum, cuda::minimum or equivalents)
Removes the thrust::unary_function base classes instead of re-defining them

evals.prompt: This project in code/ built fine with CUDA 12.6. With CUDA 13 the .cpp files fail with 'thrust/host_vector.h: No such file or directory'. Fix the build properly (don't hardcode paths), run it, and tell me what changed in CUDA 13 that broke it.
evals.expected_output: Explains that CUDA 13 moved the bundled CCCL headers (Thrust, CUB, libcu++) from <ctk>/include to <ctk>/include/cccl, which nvcc adds automatically but the host C++ compiler does not, so .cpp files that include Thrust or cuda/std headers fail. Fixes CMake by linking a target that carries the include path: find_package(CUDAToolkit) + CUDA::cudart (or CUDA::toolkit), or find_package(CCCL) + CCCL::CCCL together with CUDA::cudart; propagated PUBLIC from fleet_gpu or added to fleet_report. Does not hardcode /usr/local/cuda paths and does not change includes to <cccl/thrust/...>. Builds with CMake and runs, printing fleet mean=49.950 max=99.9.
assertions: Explains that CUDA 13 moved the CCCL headers into include/cccl, which only nvcc adds automatically
Fixes the build with an imported CMake target (CUDA::cudart / CUDA::toolkit, or CCCL::CCCL plus the CUDA runtime) rather than hardcoded paths
Does not rewrite includes as <cccl/thrust/...>
Builds and runs the project and reports fleet mean=49.950 max=99.9

evals.prompt: Binning in code/bin_particles.cu (sorting particles by grid cell every step) is the bottleneck of our simulation. Make the sort as fast as you can on this GPU while keeping particles ordered by cell. Report before/after sort time per step and explain what made the original slow.
evals.expected_output: Explains that thrust::sort with a custom lambda comparator over 28-byte structs cannot use radix sort and falls back to a comparison (merge) sort that moves the whole struct. Instead extracts the cell ids into a key array and sorts (key, index) pairs with radix sort (thrust::sort_by_key with default less, or cub::DeviceRadixSort::SortPairs), then gathers/permutes the particles once; since cell ids are below 65536, restricts the radix sort to bits [0,16) with begin_bit/end_bit to halve the passes. Reuses buffers/temp storage across steps. Measured sort time drops several times (about 9 ms to under 2 ms on an RTX 4090), and the result is still ordered by cell.
assertions: Explains that sorting the structs with a custom comparator cannot use radix sort and falls back to a slower comparison (merge) sort
Sorts integer cell keys with radix sort (sort_by_key / cub::DeviceRadixSort) and permutes the particles with an index gather (or equivalent key-value sort)
Restricts the radix sort to the 16 significant key bits (begin_bit/end_bit), or explains why it chose not to
Verifies the particles are still ordered by cell
Reports measured before and after sort times, with the new sort several times faster

evals.prompt: code/pipeline.cu processes 8 independent channels, each on its own stream, but nsys shows no overlap between the streams at all. Make the channels actually run concurrently and the whole thing faster. Keep the printed checksum the same, and tell me why the streams didn't overlap.
evals.expected_output: Explains that Thrust algorithms with thrust::cuda::par.on(stream) synchronize the stream before returning, and that thrust::transform_reduce returns its value to the host, which blocks too (plus per-call temp allocation with cudaMalloc/cudaFree, which synchronizes the device). Switches to thrust::cuda::par_nosync.on(stream) for the transform and writes the reduction results into device memory without blocking (thrust::reduce_into with a transform_iterator, or cub::DeviceReduce::TransformReduce/Reduce on the stream with preallocated temp storage), synchronizing only once at the end and copying the energies back in bulk. The checksum stays 26754811.958 and the measured runtime drops (about 2x or more).

Explains that transform_reduce returns its result to the host, which blocks on every call
Uses thrust::cuda::par_nosync.on(stream) or CUB calls on the stream so the host does not block per step

evals.prompt: Please review code/ingest.cu for correctness bugs before we ship it. Fix everything you find, run it, and tell me what was wrong.
evals.expected_output: Finds and fixes five silent bugs: (1) thrust::reduce over device_vector<bool> accumulates in bool and returns 1 instead of the count; use thrust::count or reduce with an int init. (2) thrust::exclusive_scan over the uint8_t per-sensor counts without an init accumulates in uint8_t and wraps at 256; pass an int init 0 (or widen the input). (3) The radix sort restricts the bit range to 11 bits, but the drift keys are signed and negative values need the sign bit; sort all bits (or offset the keys to be non-negative before using a reduced bit range). (4) After sorting with a cub::DoubleBuffer the sorted keys are in keys.Current(), which may be drift_alt, but the median is read from drift. (5) cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce::Min uses numeric_limits<float>::max() as its identity, so all-+inf (offline) sensors come out as FLT_MAX and are not counted as offline; use DeviceSegmentedReduce::Reduce with cuda::minimum and a +infinity init. After the fixes the program prints valid readings 2879077 of 3200000, last sensor offset 2879020, median drift 0, offline sensors 516.
assertions: Fixes the bool-mask thrust::reduce count (bool accumulator returns 1)
Fixes the uint8_t exclusive_scan accumulator overflow with an int init or wider input
Fixes the radix sort of signed drift keys restricted to 11 bits (sorts all bits or offsets keys to non-negative)
Reads the sorted keys from the DoubleBuffer's Current() buffer instead of the original drift array
Fixes the per-sensor minimum so offline (all +inf) sensors stay +inf (explicit +inf init instead of DeviceSegmentedReduce::Min)

evals.prompt: code/ledger.cu totals trade amounts per account. Our audit reruns it and compares the totals bit for bit, and it flags differences even though the input is identical and it's the same GPU (the program prints how many of 20 reruns differ). Run it and tell me what caused the differences.

Replaces it with a reduction that has a fixed combination order: cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce::Sum over per-account begin/end offsets (run_to_run deterministic by default), with the offsets derived from the sorted account ids (vectorized lower_bound/upper_bound, run-length encode, or unique + counts; integer work is deterministic). Accumulation stays in float. After the change the program prints accounts: 160, reruns that differ bitwise: 0 of 20, a max relative error vs the double reference that is still around 1e-7, and a time per call in the same range as before (about 0.2-0.4 ms vs 0.16 ms on an RTX 4090).
assertions: Explains that reduce_by_key combines partial sums of long key runs in an order that varies between runs
Replaces reduce_by_key with a reduction that has a fixed combination order (cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce over per-account offsets, or an equivalent)
Keeps the totals as float sums (no double or fixed-point accumulation)
Runs the program and shows 0 of 20 reruns differ, with the max relative error still below 1e-5
Reports the time per call, which stays within a few times the original

evals.prompt: code/replay.cu computes the net effect of an event log on the GPU, but the register value doesn't match the CPU replay (it prints MISMATCH). Find out why and fix it. The composition has to stay on the GPU (no host loop over the events). Run it and explain the cause.
evals.expected_output: Explains that thrust::reduce (like cub::DeviceReduce) requires the binary operator to be commutative as well as associative: the GPU reduction combines partial results out of order, and composing updates (Then) is associative but not commutative, so the result is silently wrong even though nothing errors. Fixes it with an algorithm that preserves operand order for associative operators: thrust::inclusive_scan(log.begin(), log.end(), out.begin(), Then{}) (or cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveScan) and taking the last element, optionally writing through a discarding/last-element output to avoid the extra array, or an equivalent order-preserving reduction on the GPU. The Then operator keeps its meaning. After the fix the program prints register after replay: gpu=3279595927 cpu=3279595927 -> MATCH.
assertions: Explains that thrust::reduce needs a commutative operator and reorders operands, and that composing the updates is associative but not commutative
Fixes it on the GPU with an order-preserving algorithm (thrust::inclusive_scan / cub::DeviceScan and taking the last element, or an equivalent), without a host loop over the events

(<cuda/launch>), passing the buffers as cuda::std::span<float>; the result is copied back with cuda::copy_bytes(stream, buffer, host_vector) (<cuda/algorithm>) or an equivalent libcu++ copy, followed by stream.sync(). No cudaMalloc, cudaStreamCreate or <<<>>> remain. It builds with nvcc -std=c++17 (or c++20), runs, and the check against the expected y values passes.

Allocates the device buffers with cuda::make_buffer / cuda::buffer from cuda::device_default_memory_pool (no cudaMalloc)
Launches the kernels with cuda::launch and a cuda::make_config configuration (no <<<...>>>)

evals.prompt: Quick one: we're on CUDA 13.4 (CCCL 3.5). Show me the cub::DeviceTopK call to get the 100 largest floats and their indices out of a 50M-element device array on a given cudaStream_t. Can I just pass the stream as the last argument like with other CUB algorithms? Is the output sorted?
evals.expected_output: Shows cub::DeviceTopK::MaxPairs (from <cub/device/device_topk.cuh>) with either the single-call form or the two-phase temp storage pattern, a counting iterator (cuda::make_counting_iterator(0) or thrust::counting_iterator) as the values to get indices, and an execution environment that combines cuda::stream_ref{stream} with cuda::execution::require(cuda::execution::determinism::not_guaranteed, cuda::execution::output_ordering::unsorted). Explains that in CCCL 3.5 DeviceTopK only supports non-deterministic, unsorted output and a call without these requirements (e.g. relying on the default environment or passing a raw stream) fails to compile with a static_assert. States that the 100 results are not sorted and must be sorted afterwards (e.g. thrust::sort_by_key on the k pairs with a greater comparator) if order matters.
assertions: Uses cub::DeviceTopK::MaxPairs with a counting iterator (or index array) as values
Passes an environment that requires determinism::not_guaranteed and output_ordering::unsorted
States that passing only the stream (without those requirements) does not compile in CCCL 3.5
States that the output is unsorted and shows or describes sorting the k results if order is needed

evals.prompt: Is cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum (or thrust::inclusive_scan) over floats bitwise reproducible from run to run on the same GPU? If not, what's the cheapest fix that keeps everything in float, and what does it cost in speed? We're on CUDA 13.
evals.expected_output: No: the default single-pass decoupled look-back scan combines partial sums in a timing-dependent order, so float results can differ in the last bits between runs (cub::DeviceScan's default determinism is not_guaranteed; DeviceReduce by contrast defaults to run_to_run). Cheapest fix in CCCL 3.x (CUDA 13): call cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum(d_in, d_out, n, env) with env = cuda::std::execution::env{cuda::stream_ref{stream}, cuda::execution::require(cuda::execution::determinism::run_to_run)}, which keeps float and costs essentially nothing. gpu_to_gpu is only supported for integral scans. Fixed-point/double or hand-written scans are not necessary.
assertions: Says the default float scan is not run-to-run reproducible because of timing-dependent (decoupled look-back) combination order
Recommends cuda::execution::require(cuda::execution::determinism::run_to_run) passed to cub::DeviceScan through an environment
Does not present fixed-point, double, or a hand-written scan as the primary fix
States that the run_to_run scan costs little or nothing in speed

evals.prompt: We compute cumulative exposure with an inclusive prefix sum over ~50M floats using CUB. The output must be bit-identical between our A100 and H100 nodes (CUDA 13, CCCL 3.5). Can I just pass the gpu_to_gpu determinism requirement to cub::DeviceScan::InclusiveSum? If not, what should I do, and what are the trade-offs?
evals.expected_output: No for float: in CCCL 3.5 cub::DeviceScan accepts determinism::gpu_to_gpu only for integral types with known operators; passing it for a float scan fails to compile with a static_assert. (run_to_run is supported for float scans and fixes same-GPU reruns, but not cross-architecture differences.) To get identical bits across A100 and H100, convert to fixed-point integers (e.g. int64 via llrint(x * scale) in a transform iterator), run the integer scan (optionally requiring gpu_to_gpu, which integral scans support), and convert back; integer addition is associative and exact so results match on every GPU, at the cost of quantization to the chosen scale and a range check. Alternatively use a fixed, architecture-independent scan order, but not just double precision.
assertions: States that gpu_to_gpu is not available for float DeviceScan in CCCL 3.5 (integral types only; compile-time error)
Recommends scanning fixed-point/integer values (exact, associative) to get identical bits across architectures
Notes that run_to_run (or the default) does not fix cross-architecture differences, or that double alone does not
Mentions the quantization/range trade-off of the fixed-point approach

evals.prompt: I sum every row of a row-major float matrix on the GPU, 4M rows x 16 columns, with cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce::Sum(d_in, d_out, num_rows, d_offsets, d_offsets + 1) where d_offsets is 0, 16, 32, ... (CCCL 3.5, RTX 4090). It takes about 3.5 ms for 64M floats, far slower than a plain cub::DeviceReduce over the same data. Why, and what should I call instead? Show the exact call. And what would you use if the rows had different (still small) lengths?
evals.expected_output: The offset-based overload of cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce schedules work per segment (a thread block per segment), which suits large segments but wastes almost all of each block on 16-element rows, so millions of tiny segments are slow. For uniform segments CCCL 3.x has a fixed-size overload that needs no offsets: cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce::Sum(d_in, d_out, num_segments, segment_size), i.e. Sum(d_in, d_out, 4000000, 16) (also Min/Max/Reduce, and a two-phase form with temp storage); it takes about 0.37 ms for this input, roughly 10x faster. For variable-length small segments, thrust::reduce_by_key with one key per item (row ids built once from the offsets with a vectorized upper_bound, or scatter + scan) is about 6x faster than the offsets overload (0.7 ms vs 4.7 ms for 4M segments averaging 16 items); the offsets overload is the right choice again once segments have hundreds of items or more. A hand-written kernel is not needed.
assertions: Explains that the offset-based overload handles each segment separately (per-segment thread block / overhead), which is inefficient for millions of tiny segments
Shows the fixed-size overload with the correct name and arguments: cub::DeviceSegmentedReduce::Sum(d_in, d_out, num_segments, segment_size), optionally with temp storage or an environment
For variable-length small segments recommends thrust::reduce_by_key (or cub::DeviceReduce::ReduceByKey) with a key per item rather than a hand-written kernel

evals.prompt: We have C++17 code that calls std::transform, std::reduce and std::count_if with std::execution::par. On CUDA 13.4 (CCCL 3.5), can libcu++ run those on the GPU with the same std-style calls? Show the headers, the execution policy, how to make them run on a specific cudaStream_t, and what the iterators have to point to.
evals.expected_output: Yes. Since CCCL 3.4 (CUDA 13.4) libcu++ implements the standard parallel algorithms in namespace cuda::std with a CUDA backend selected by the cuda::execution::gpu policy: #include <cuda/std/execution> plus <cuda/std/algorithm> and <cuda/std/numeric>, then e.g. cuda::std::reduce(cuda::execution::gpu, first, last, 0.0f), cuda::std::transform(cuda::execution::gpu, first, last, out, op), cuda::std::count_if(cuda::execution::gpu, first, last, pred). Only the gpu policy has a backend: cuda::std::execution::par / seq with these algorithms is a compile error. To run on a stream attach it to the policy: auto policy = cuda::execution::gpu.with(cuda::get_stream, stream) where stream is a cuda::stream, cuda::stream_ref{raw} or a cudaStream_t (<cuda/stream> / <cuda/stream_ref>); a memory resource for temporaries is attached the same way with .with(cuda::mr::get_memory_resource, pool). The iterators must be random-access iterators into device-accessible memory (device pointers, thrust::device_vector iterators, libcu++ fancy iterators), not host std::vector iterators. The file is compiled by nvcc as CUDA, and lambdas need __host__ __device__ (or __device__) with --extended-lambda. Thrust (thrust::reduce with thrust::cuda::par.on(stream)) remains the alternative for older toolkits.
assertions: Says yes: libcu++ provides cuda::std:: parallel algorithms that run on the GPU with the cuda::execution::gpu policy
Names the headers: <cuda/std/execution> together with <cuda/std/algorithm> and/or <cuda/std/numeric>
Shows attaching the stream to the policy with cuda::execution::gpu.with(cuda::get_stream, stream)
States that the iterators must be random-access iterators into device-accessible memory (device pointers or device_vector iterators), not host containers

evals.prompt: CUDA 13.4 / CCCL 3.5. I have a sorted device array of 200M int keys and only need the number of distinct keys, not the keys themselves. What's the call that doesn't write a compacted copy anywhere? Show the code.
evals.expected_output: Use thrust::unique_count(thrust::device, d_keys, d_keys + n) (<thrust/unique.h>), which counts the runs of equal consecutive elements without producing any output; for sorted keys that is the number of distinct keys. Equivalent alternatives that also write nothing: counting adjacent differences with thrust::inner_product(first, last - 1, first + 1, 1, plus, not_equal_to) or a count_if over a zip of neighbours, or cub::DeviceSelect::Unique / thrust::unique_copy into thrust::make_discard_iterator() / cuda::discard_iterator. evals.prompt: nvidia-smi on our server shows 'CUDA Version: 12.4' in the header but nvcc --version says 13.4, and my program built with that nvcc fails at startup with 'CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version'. What is going on and how do I fix it?
evals.expected_output: The version in the nvidia-smi header is the highest CUDA version the installed driver supports, not the installed toolkit. The toolkit (nvcc, libcudart 13.4) is newer than what the driver supports, so cudart refuses to initialize (cudaErrorInsufficientDriver). Fix it by upgrading the NVIDIA driver to one that supports CUDA 13.4 (and rebooting or reloading the kernel modules), or by building against a CUDA 12.x toolkit that the current driver supports, or by running in a container with a matching toolkit on a host with a new enough driver. This does not involve CCCL.
assertions: Explains that the nvidia-smi header shows the maximum CUDA version supported by the driver, not the toolkit version
Recommends upgrading the driver (or using a toolkit version the driver supports)
